text: CONTENTS  - 1983 POLICY SPEECH.  - BUDGET COST OF NEW INITIATIVES.  - SUPPLEMENTARY STATEMENTS.  1983 POLICY SPEECH  Australians have never had a clearer choice than at this election. It is the Liberal Party that is preserving and building a free society. It is the Liberal Party that is working to fulfil the hopes of all Australians. It is the Liberal Party alone that can keep building for the future. We govern for all Australians whether their families have lived here for, generations or only a few years. We encourage all Australians to contribute their best to the best nation on earth.  This election gives Australians a choice between the certainty of recovery under this Government, and insecurity under the riskiest and most divisive Labor Party in our history. It presents a choice between the wages pause, supported by eight governments and the nation's wage tribunals, and Labor's attempts to destroy that pause.  The nation asked for Labor's cooperation. It got a callous rebuff. This is an election about responsibility, about the security that only responsibility can bring. Australia can't afford the turmoil and insecurity of the Federal Labor Party. It needs the secure program which the Government offers which will build Australia by helping people and widening opportunities.  Since 1975 our policies have done much to rebuild Australia. Because of our policies, Australia was one of the last countries hit by the world recession. Before the world recession hit us, we revitalized confidence in the economy. We brought down inflation. 455,000 new jobs were created. Australia's output rose more than the average of advanced countries. New private investment rose almost 50% in real terms. Development was proceeding on a great scale.  When the world recession finally did hit Australia its effect was greatly worsened by two things. The drought is one of the worst in Australia's history, and it is affecting us all.  And in the last year or two Australia has suffered a totally unjustified wages explosion, brought about by ACTU policies laid down when the present leader of the Labor Party was its president. The world recession would have done Australia far less damage if the unions had not pushed their demands for higher wages and shorter hours beyond the endurance of industry.  This election will decide whether Australia goes the Labor way, with rampant union power, soaring inflation and worsening unemployment, or whether Australia puts the recession behind it and gets back on the road of more jobs and rising living standards.  We saw the recession coming and took positive action. Even though we are affected by what happens in the rest of the world, the Government will help Australia to create its own future. We're not waiting for the world.  At a time of difficulty, we have helped Australian families. The family is the rock on which our future will be built. We helped in last year's family Budget, cutting personal taxes, improving rebates on home interest payments. Over two years we have increased all family allowances by 50%. Our family Budget put $18 a week into the hands of typical Australian families. We helped low income families especially, with our innovative family income supplement, and extra help to keep children at school.  We will adjust unemployment benefits for single people over 18 in line with other pensions and benefits in May. The Government strongly believes in child care. In the Budget we lifted funding by almost 50%. We will expand that program by providing 150 new child care projects. We helped the older members of our families. The family Budget increased the income limits for pensions, and expanded rental assistance. To give further support to pensioners; we will increase access to the health benefits card, with a substantial further increase in the income limits. No Budget has ever done more to help Australia's families. We are the family party.  The family Budget helps young people. We raised student allowances and boosted our manpower and training programs to $250 million. These programs will directly assist a quarter of a million Australians, most of them young people. Money from the wage pause is now helping many more young people to find jobs and opportunities. We are determined to do everything possible to help young Australians. We know the future of the best country in the world depends on them.  We will establish a special youth project in reforestation and conservation. We will establish further youth projects for people not adequately assisted by present programs. This will include women, Aboriginal and people disadvantaged by physical or language difficulties. On top of these programs, we have decided to offer 10,000 additional places over two years in the Defense Services for young men and women partly because more people are applying for Defense positions than there are places. This project will be based on a one year voluntary enlistment in the Armed Services.  In addition to basic training, as many as possible of those who join will receive relevant trade training, which our Services have a capacity to provide. Those who join this program will be doing something for themselves and for Australia. It promises a worthwhile experience for thousands of young Australians.  Throughout 1982 we positively assisted home buyers. Through our actions an extra $1.2 billion is going into housing, and with lower interest rates these policies are having increased impact.  We have done much to assist Australia's industries. There are vastly improved depreciation schedules to encourage industry to buy modern equipment. We took action against dumping and established the "Buy Australia" campaign.  Just before Christmas, in an historic meeting, we brought Commonwealth and State governments together on the wage pause, and I want to thank Doug Anthony and John Howard for getting it in place.  It is a wage pause with a difference: it expresses the Australian ideal of mate ship. The wage pause gives people with jobs a chance to help other Australians without jobs. The savings from Commonwealth wages are helping the young unemployed get jobs, and older people who have been retrenched.  The pause lets wage and salary earners help themselves by keeping prices down and protecting their own jobs. Above all, the wage pause will lower inflation and help make our industries more competitive and profitable, and this will mean more jobs.  This Government worked hard to achieve that historic wage pause agreement. Eight governments agreed, the Arbitration Commission agreed, most Australians agreed. But the ACTU and the Federal Labor Party rejected it.  How can they talk of bringing Australians together when they are the only ones out of step. They are determined to destroy the pause, with nothing to put in its place.  They have incited strikes in the oil industry. Strikes in that industry over the last year cost $600 million in lost revenue and a further $700 million for additional imports.  The wage pause is enormously important to Australia's recovery. The Labor Party has been totally divisive, totally contemptuous of the unemployed, totally unconcerned about Australia's long term economic security.  In 1983 Australia needs responsible policies, not division. Strong, reliable economic management is the heart of effective government in today's difficult world, but the achievements of this Government go much further. Our concern for fairness led us to stamp out tax avoidance. In the interests of fairness we will continue our drive for tax reform.  Our concern to hunt down organized crime led us to establish the National Crimes Commission.  Our concern about the drought led us to establish comprehensive drought relief arrangements. We will continue the drought interest subsidy for a year beyond the lifting of the drought. We will make sure there is enough finance to help keep people on their farms, to enable crops to be planted. We will introduce a new rural research program to help farmers lower their costs, and a new  five year soil conservation and afforestation program.  Our concern for the environment led to our offer to the Tasmanian Government to equalize the cost of power and put off the Franklin Dam. That offer remains open. We now commit $50 million over five years to a great national park in South West Tasmania, so that it can be enjoyed and preserved for our children.  In taking these measures we are building for the future. We believe the Government can do things to help bring out the very best in Australians.  The Commonwealth Games were a great success, and we all felt great pride in our sportsmen and women. We will help them build on their achievements by adding to the Sports Institute's programs, and set up a center for the Institute in Perth.  We have established centers of excellence for research in universities. Australia has some of the best medical scientists in the world and we have provided them with generous research funds. Our scientists are on the verge of a breakthrough for an anti-malaria vaccine. Our objective must be to bring this to completion and to achieve the development in Australia. Over the next three years, we will increase funding for our medical scientists by a further 30% in real terms.  We also want the best artistic achievements to be shown in every State. We will set up a National Arts Touring Fund under the Australia Council.  Through these initiatives we are leading Australia. We are building for the future, we are not waiting for the world.  At a time of falling private investment, we are building for the future by establishing a program of great national projects.  Our Bicentennial Road Program will modernize and build up Australia's road network. To reduce transport costs further, we will provide standard gauge rail access to a number of ports in Victoria and Queensland.  We will explore with Victoria and South Australia the scope for an early start on an electricity grid to balance out demand and give greater security of supply in both States.  Our Bicentennial Water Resources Program will mean better use of our scarce water supplies. Every State will benefit and thousands of jobs will be generated. Projects in the Murray/Murrumbidgee Basin will improve the quality and flow of water. We are determining the site for a major new dam on the Upper Murray.  We are exploring the age old dream of turning the coastal rivers of New South Wales and Queensland inland to see if it can be turned into reality for our children.  The Darwin-Alice Springs railway will be completed by 1988. This should greatly assist the steel industry at Whyalla, and greatly assist South Australia generally as well as the Northern Territory.  There are other Bicentennial projects: programs for the arts; the new Australian telescope, to develop further the skills of our astronomers; the Bicentennial Program itself, in which all Australians will participate. The Bicentenary will make Australians proud of Australia's achievements, and our capacity to live and work together.  We are a nation built by people from every land. We will keep working to improve the quality of Australian multiculturalism and a fair go for all Australians.  We are looking ahead to 1988 and beyond.  The jobs of the future will depend upon innovation and enterprise. Businesses need encouragement to adopt innovative practices, create new products and markets. We will provide this encouragement in partnership with business.  We will set up an Advanced Technology Corporation to help small and medium firms develop innovative products and services. The Corporation will help innovators assess their proposals and organize venture capital. It will help them find product development facilities to put their ideas into practice, and it will help them with market research and information.  To attract investment to new high risk ventures, we will grant 100% tax deductibility for investments in projects approved through the Corporation, to an overall limit of $100 m in the initial operations.  Small business has a vital role in generating new employment, products and ideas. We will introduce a new preferential tax rate 5 cents below the standard rate for small companies with taxable incomes below $100000, and provide $25 m additional funding through a new division of the Development Bank specifically to assist small business.  As part of our program of encouraging Australia's industrial development, we will make advance payments of 10% on Government purchases of Australian manufactured products, and extend the Export Promotion Scheme. These initiatives will assist business, in partnership with government, to build the foundation for our future economic growth and employment.  Good industrial relations are vital to the future of our country. This Government has shown its willingness to consult and work with the unions, not for them, as Labor does.  This Government intends to govern for all Australians. It will continue to seek cooperation with all parties, including the ACTU but it will not tolerate attempts by the militant few to impose on the majority.  We have introduced effective reforms to the Conciliation and Arbitration Act within our existing industrial relations powers. But we believe these powers are too limited in certain key areas. We will therefore seek power through a referendum for the Commonwealth to legislate to give the Conciliation and Arbitration Commission power to make sure awards and agreements are not broken, and to enable the Commission, and the Government where necessary, to prevent the community being denied essential services by the abuse of union power - powers which we hope would not have to be used.  As a further measure, our legislation for secret ballots will be extended and made more effective. In the protection of essential services and vital national industries we will legislate to enable secret ballots to be ordered in respect of proposed strike action, and we will require secret ballots for the election of all senior union office bearers, to be conducted at public expense by the Electoral Commissioner.  These powers are not to confront, but to protect all Australians and the democratic rights of all union members. They are needed to increase the confidence and security that will underlie economic recovery.  In looking to the future, nothing is more important than education. All Australian children must be equipped with relevant training and the skills they will need in a complex world.  We reject as totally divisive and wrong Labor's policy to deny the basic right of every Australian child to some Government support for his or her education. We want to tackle the real causes of dissatisfaction with the education system, and get more children to stay at school longer.  Education needs to give all our children better opportunities to do the things they do well. The Schools Commission has pointed in the past to an over-reliance on academic curriculums. That suits academically-inclined students, but there are many other students who also deserve a fair go.  We will provide $25 m on a dollar for dollar basis with the States, for counseling for younger students and parents, and for reform of curriculums. This will help meet the needs of all children.  We will also ask the Tertiary Education Commission to report on whether there are adequate places and opportunities available in tertiary education. We will invite the States to join us in promoting the use of computers in all Australian schools, with a Commonwealth contribution of $20 m a year for five years from 1984. We will provide a further $35 m over the next three years to help increase new places in non government schools.  In foreign policy, Australia's stature as a middle power has increased the range of our international activities and the weight of our responsibilities.  Our aid program which is concentrated in South East Asia and the South Pacific, contributes to stability in our region. ANZUS and the wider western alliance are central to our foreign policy, and Australia has a significant part to play.  We have a proud record of contributing to peace-keeping in world trouble spots most recently in Sinai, and we give active support to responsible disarmament measures. We have worked through the Commonwealth, especially in the  Commonwealth Meetings and helping bring peace to Zimbabwe.  Australia's voice is heard with respect in the Commonwealth and around the world. Some units of our armed forces are stationed at Butterworth in Malaysia. The Mirages now based there are being phased out, and subject to discussions with the Government of Malaysia, we will replace them with a squadron of our new FA/18 fighter planes.  This illustrates our practical support for the Five Power Defense Arrangements and symbolizes our cooperation with countries in our region. Under this Government, Australia has become a vital link in the interlocking security arrangements safeguarding the free world.  One great danger of world recession is that countries will raise trade barriers against each other. In these circumstances, an experienced government with a personal knowledge of other countries can do much to protect Australia's interests. For example, in 1974 Australia was totally excluded from the Japanese meat market. Negotiations on new trade agreements between Japan and the United States are currently proceeding. We will make sure that Australia's interests are protected.  Through all the years the Labor Party has taken a negative approach to the Commonwealth, our alliances, our role in speaking against aggression, and our efforts to liberalize world trade. In that approach there is no security for Australia.  In this election the choice is clear.  Is Australia to work in a common cause for recovery, or will it support those who want to break the wages pause? Australia wants a government which will work with union leaders, not a Labor Government which will work for the unions and increased union power.  This Government will strengthen our alliances - a Labor Government would undermine our defense arrangements. Australia wants a government which will maintain the security and stability of our institutions at a time when we most need them, not a Labor Government which through its recently amended Platform is now committed to challenging those institutions and turning Australia into a republic.  Australia must have a government of prudent managers with stability, and a vision of the future, not the spend, spend, spend philosophy of Labor. No-one wants a return to the chaos and insecurity of the Whitlam years. The first act was enough without waiting for the second.  We must make recovery certain for Australia. This nation is too great to be shackled by Labor's divisiveness and irrelevance. We are building for the future, we are creating Australia. We do not underestimate the difficulties but we know our policies will make this a better land. And we can take pride that it is the Government team that has put these policies together, in areas of major innovation-John Carrick in the water resources program; Ralph Hunt, developing the great program for roads; Andrew Peacock, proposing major innovations in industry; Ian Macphee, conciliator, negotiator but a person who can act from firmness and real conviction, proposing major innovations in industrial relations.  We are building Australia with our policies. We are building Australia with our vision. We are building Australia with the determination of Australians. We are not waiting for the World.  BUDGET COST OF NEW INITIATIVES AND PROPOSALS ANNOUNCED IN POLICY SPEECH AND DOCUMENTS  1983 policy speech  SUPPLEMENTARY STATEMENTS  ECONOMIC POLICIES FOR RECOVERY  AUSTRALIA'S ECONOMIC POSITION  The Government's economic policies are based on:  - an effective anti-inflationary strategy which recognizes the importance of monetary, fiscal and other policy elements.  - encouragement of the growth of industries and the development of resources.  - directing of priorities towards an economic environment which fosters sound economic growth and increased employment.  These policies have had much to do with the economy's ability to sustain a remarkably strong rate of growth during the early stages of the present severe worldwide recession. Strong business investment, a high level of consumer confidence and a rate of inflation that was lower than most of our major trading partners underpinned a growth rate of 4.1 per cent in GNP in 1981, compared with an average growth of only 0.7 per cent in the OECD countries. The protracted nature of the overseas recession made it inevitable that Australia would ultimately feel its impact. Over 1982 activity continued to be weak in all of the major industrial countries, and there was an average drop of  1 / 2  per cent in gross national product of countries in the OECD area. In the seven major OECD economies, industrial production dropped by 4 1 / 2  per cent in real terms in 1982 and unemployment rose everywhere. In North America, there were twelve million unemployed at the end of 1982, in the European countries of the OECD, 16 million.  The ultimate effects on the Australian economy of this strong world downturn were magnified by two domestic factors:  - probably the worst drought in a century.  - the lagged effect of two years of sharply increasing wage costs.  About 80 per cent of the farms in the eastern mainland States are drought affected and real gross farm product could decline in 1982-83 by about 20 per cent. Because of subdued farm prices and rising wage costs, the decline in farm incomes in real terms could be as much as 50 per cent. This sharp fall in income is already affecting rural service industries, rural supply manufacturers and rural employment. However, the effects of a decline in export income from meat and wheat have yet to be felt.  The sharpness of recent labor cost rises can be seen in the fact that over the two years to the September quarter of 1982, average weekly earnings for male employees increased by 29.7 per cent, whereas in the same period the Consumer Price Index increased by 22.4 and manufacturing output prices by only 18.1 per cent.  It is no accident that the unemployment rate has risen sharply with this increase in real labor costs and with the resulting decrease in business profits.  Nor is it an accident that Australia's inflation performance has moved from being better than the OECD average two years ago to now being much worse.  Two years ago, the average rate of inflation in the OECD area was about 13.6 per cent. It is now down to around 7 per cent while Australia's is about 11 per cent.  It is vital to Australia's economic recovery and to its ability to take full advantage of a resumption of world economic growth that our industries become competitive with those overseas.  The link between rising wages, falling company profitability and rising unemployment, is clear and unmistakable.  THE GOVERNMENT'S WAGE PAUSE INITIATIVE  The Government's wage pause initiative recognized the severe squeeze on profits which had occurred over the previous two years and was designed to protect the job security of Australians. The public sector savings from the pause were directed towards employment-related activities. The Government believes that the great majority of the 90 per cent or more of the labor force who have jobs are prepared to sacrifice the prospect of a wage increase to try to help those who do not have jobs or whose job security might be threatened.  There has obviously been recognition by the average Australian worker of the need for wage moderation and widespread community support for the Government's program to slow wage costs, restore business profitability and expend Government savings from the wage pause to help both the young and adult unemployed.  The program has been endorsed by State Governments of all political persuasions, by the Arbitration Commission and by a very widespread section of the community.  REFORM OF THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM  The Government commissioned an Inquiry into the Australian Financial System early in 1979 with a view to improving the efficiency and flexibility of the Australian financial system. In its final Report the Campbell Committee recommended that such objectives would best be achieved by a less regulated, more competitive financial system, with greater freedom of entry, subject to the maintenance of prudential standards necessary for the continuation of investor confidence in the stability of the system as a whole, and banks in particular. Before and after the release of the Campbell Committee Report, the Government has taken a number of important steps with the intention of increasing the flexibility of bank operations and thus their relative competitiveness. Other measures taken include:  - introduction of a tender system of marketing Treasury Notes and Bonds which has provided more flexibility in the marketing arrangements for Commonwealth securities.  - removal of the limits on the amount that could be invested overseas in equity and real estate and other measures to ease exchange controls on overseas transactions.  - action to reduce government involvement in the financial system, including the endorsement of the proposed private industry-based deposit insurance scheme for permanent building societies, and the decision to sell the assets and business of the Housing Loans Insurance Corporation to the private sector.  In January 1983 the Government announced that it would allow the initial entry of around ten banks into the Australian banking system. The Government believes this decision will have major implications for the efficiency and competitiveness of the financial system yielding benefits for all bank customers.  INCENTIVES AND ASSISTANCE  In the last Budget, and immediately before, the Government sought to provide as much assistance, relief and incentive as it responsibly could to those who have been caused real hardship by economic circumstances.  - Personal taxation cuts, which came into effect last November, have provided some immediate assistance to every PAYEE taxpayer.  - People who are buying their own homes have been receiving taxation rebates on their mortgage interest payments.  - Family allowances have been increased by 50 per cent for first and second children.  - Together these Budget measures have put up to $20 per week into the pockets of qualifying wage earners.  - Home-buyers have been additionally assisted by an improved home savings grant scheme, an undertaking by nationally operating banks to provide an additional $400 million for new housing loans and an agreement by savings banks to develop low start mortgages. These measures are also giving a boost to the housing industry.  - The manufacturing, mining and rural industries have been helped by other measures: more generous depreciation provisions, a continuation of the industrial research and development scheme, and a significant strengthening of the export marketing scheme.  - Small businesses have been especially assisted by another increase in the retention allowance for private companies. Since this Government took office the retention allowance has been increased from 50 per cent to 80 per cent.  - Total outlays for industry assistance and development this year are budgeted to exceed one billion dollars. The severe drought has major implications for all of us. The Government has provided generous assistance to those worst affected by the drought.  TAXATION  The Government's taxation objectives are two-fold:  - keeping taxes as low as responsible economic management and community needs will allow.  - distributing the burden of taxation as fairly as possible, with particular concern for low income families.  This Government has shown by its record a very great concern for the fairness of the taxation system and the effects of the taxation system on personal incentives. Although the overall taxation burden in Australia is relatively low compared with the average among the industrial countries, our system relies more than others on direct personal taxation as a source of revenue. The Government has taken appropriate opportunities where circumstances have allowed to gradually move away from over reliance on personal tax and to alter the taxation mix in a way which is fair to all taxpayers.  No government has worked harder than this one at stamping out tax avoidance and tax evasion, in order to make the tax system as fair as possible.  - This Government drafted and introduced new general anti-avoidance legislation which has rapidly ended the promotion of artificial tax avoidance schemes.  - Taxation penalties have been stiffened criminal penalties.  - Legislation has been brought in to recover tax evaded from earlier bottom of the harbor strips of untaxed company profits.  - Legislation has been amended in order to crack down on international profit shifting arrangements.  - Taxation penalties have been stiffened for offences such as abuse of deferral and dispute provisions.  - The cash economy is now being attacked by introducing a system of tax withholding at source of income for payments for labor and services in certain industries where evasion poses particular problems.  ECONOMIC PROSPECTS  The average Australian recognizes that world economic health is a pre-requisite to economic growth and prosperity in Australia. Given responsible economic policies, Australia can expect to again see its economy grow and the living standards of its citizens rise. No-one should succumb to the temptation of believing that there is some easy road to economic buoyancy, some magical way of creating money that doesn't come out of taxpayers pockets to spend our way to recovery. Sustainable recovery will need a continuation of the sort of responsible management this Government has on record. In recent months there have been some encouraging signs on a number of fronts:  - Interest rates have been coming down rapidly; rates on Government securities have come down by 4 or 5 per cent in the last half year, home mortgage rates and smaller overdraft rates are down by 1 per cent and prime bank lending rates have fallen by over 3 per cent.  - The Balance of Payments is improving; in December Australia's trade deficit was smaller than for nineteen months and there was an overall balance of payments surplus for the fourth consecutive month. Overseas investors have been continuing to show their confidence in Australia through strong capital inflow.  - Lending for housing has been increasing rapidly; in November the number of housing loans approved by savings banks was 32 per cent higher than a year ago.  - Capital expenditure by governments has been stepped up.  EMPLOYMENT POLICY  The Government is committed to:  - assisting people in gaining employment through realistic manpower, training and retraining programs.  - ensuring that growth is not impeded by the lack of skills or training.  - promoting the growth of job opportunities for the unemployed.  Important initiatives have been introduced. These have been directed towards developing work skills so that people are better equipped to participate in the labor market. Others have been directed towards providing employment opportunities of a substantive and worthwhile nature, rather than "make work" schemes of little lasting value.  - Manpower and Training Programs have been upgraded with expenditure rising by over 20 per cent to $250 million in 1982/83 enabling over 250,000 Australians to be assisted. Initiatives in 1982/83 include:  - the increase in subsidies under work experience programs for young people  (SYETP).  - the extension of SYETP to include young people employed by State Governments.  - the extension of work experience programs to adults who have been unemployed for some time.  - the increase in CRAFT rebates for apprentices to take account of inflation and to offer an extra incentive to employers to take on more apprentices.  - the expansion in trade based pre-employment courses for apprentices.  - the increased expenditure on Youth Affairs Programs including the Community Youth Support Scheme (CYSS).  - The savings of $300 million in the Commonwealth Budget resulting from the Wages Pause are now being distributed to the States for employment-related programs. Under the $300 million Wage Pause Program:  - $100 million is being spent on welfare housing.  - $100 million will be spent on projects to assist unemployed youth.  - $100 million will be spent on projects for the older unemployed and others disadvantages in employment including Aboriginal, migrants and the disabled.  Thirty thousand persons will be directly assisted through the employment projects of the Wage Pause Program in 1983 and many more will be assisted indirectly through expenditure in supporting industries.  - The Commonwealth Employment Service is being upgraded:  - the national Job Bank computer system is being introduced progressively to enable a more efficient employment service.  - the CES office modernization program is being continued.  - 484 additional staff are being, hired to improve and extend employment services, particularly for mature age job-seekers and the long-term unemployed Aboriginal, migrants and youth.  - $2 million is to be spent on studies on the problems of the long-term unemployed, to be coordinated by the Bureau of Labor Market Research. We will continue to act with foresight and compassion.  We will introduce an additional $50 million employment program to help young people.  Accordingly, we intend to involve young people in a $20 million program in Reforestation and Conservation projects around Australia. With the conservation projects we envisage that they might range from soil conservation to the restoration of historic buildings and documents which are part of our national heritage.  We also intend to help young people who are currently not catered for adequately by present programs, either Commonwealth or State, in a $30 million program. In particular, we will be looking to initiate projects which will help those who are presently disadvantaged in the labor market including young women, Aboriginal and people disabled, physically, intellectually or linguistically.  In developing these projects, we intend to consult State governments, Local government and voluntary agencies.  In recognizing the particular difficulties of Aboriginal in the labor market, we intend, under this new program, to provide the National Aboriginal Employment Development Committee with funds to assist in its efforts to establish a better data base and to increase the effectiveness of their efforts to promote Aboriginal employment.  INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS  No government has done more to reform the Conciliation and Arbitration Act. Measures have been introduced to make union leaders more accountable to their members, to protect the rights of individuals to join or not join a union, and to overcome some of the difficulties arising from the involvement’s of State and Federal jurisdictions in the same dispute. Most recently, the law was changed to place officials of trade unions and employer organizations on the same basis as company directors regarding the discharge of their duties. These amendments followed the findings of the Royal Commissioner into the Builders Laborer’s Federation and the Federated Ship Painters and Dockers Union.  CONSULTATIVE PROCESSES.  The Government has created tripartite bodies involving trade unions, employers and Government on subjects of vital importance to industry and industrial relations.  The National Labor Consultative Council which is chaired by the Minister for Employment and Industrial relations deals with a wide range of matters including subjects such as occupational health and safety, equality of opportunity in  employment, action in respect of discrimination, and assistance for people disadvantaged in the employment market.  The National Training Council is another important body of this nature giving advice to the Minister on the entire range of training requirements.  Through the forum of the NLCC, the ACTU has accepted its responsibility for the prevention and settlement of demarcation disputes. The Government is in the process of refining the procedures for the resolution of such disputes where the ACTU is unsuccessful in doing so. These discussions will be completed as a matter of very high priority.  The Government has been vigilant in intervening in major industrial hearings to ensure that the public interest is strongly put and taken into account by industrial tribunals.  The Government has consistently consulted the ACTU and the major employer organizations prior to the preparation of each Budget and last July began what it intends to be a pattern of tripartite consultation with the ACTU and the Confederation of Australian Industry. Those discussions were conducted in a most positive and non-partisan atmosphere and had a substantial impact on Government thinking during the preparation of the Budget.  The Government will continue to seek consensus on matters of economic and social importance.  On 7 December 1982 the Government chaired a conference of State and Northern Territory Governments on the principle of a wage and salary pause. As a result, unique consensus was reached between the eight Governments of Australia, regardless of party politics. This was translated into action by a combination of legislation and submissions to Federal and State Tribunals.  Guidelines adopted both by the Federal Government in its legislation, and Arbitrate Tribunals ensured that all employees would be treated equally, and allowed to complete the current community wage round before being subject to the pause.  ENHANCEMENT OF LEGISLATIVE POWERS.  The Government intends to continue to try to find consensus with the ACTU as it has done with the State governments and with the employers.  However, no government can tolerate strikes or other industrial action in the provision of essential goods or services to the general public. Tyranny of the militant few at the cost of the majority can not be tolerated.  Interstate disputes in nationally significant industries can lead to the standing down of thousands of wage earners at the behest of greedy key workers. In those circumstances the viability of industry and commerce and the provision of a range of health and welfare services can be seriously threatened. Strategic industrial action in the oil, power, transport and pharmaceutical manufacturing industries provide ready examples of such situations.  State governments possess the power to enact essential services legislation. So do national governments throughout the world. But the industrial relations power vested in the Commonwealth by the Constitution is too limited to allow the Federal Government to validly enact such legislation. The Government will therefore seek, by way of referendum, an enlargement of its industrial relations power to enable it to legislate in order to protect the public from the abuse of union action in the provision of essential services. We would also seek to provide, under emergency services legislation, a capacity to arrange expeditiously secret ballots in respect of strikes which give rise to national crises.  Such powers would only be used as a last resort and it is to be hoped that the mere existence of the power would deter unions from abusing the privilege which society has conferred upon them. In seeking additional powers, the Government particularly wishes to confer upon the Conciliation and Arbitration Commission the capacity to enable it to secure compliance with awards which it makes or agreements which it ratifies.  Currently those awards and agreements have the status of law but compliance under their own terms can only be gained by legal proceedings before the Federal Court.  The Government has consistently sought to reform the law and administration of the Conciliation and Arbitration system to protect the rights of individuals and to make accountable to those individuals, persons who are elected to hold office in trade unions and employer organizations. Systems for the election of union officials by secret ballot have been established and after several years experience of the workings of those systems we believe it to be in the best interests of the Australian community that the rules of all trade unions and employer organizations should require officials to be elected by a secret ballot of all members of each organization under the supervision and control of the Industrial Registrar and the Electoral Commissioner. We believe it to be in the public interest to adopt this measure and for the Government to pay for the conduct of secret ballots.  HARNESSING OUR RESOURCES  RESOURCES AND ENERGY  Australia has firmly established itself under this Government as one of the world's greatest exporters of mineral and energy resources.  This has brought immense benefits to Australians, and the Government is convinced that continued development of the national resources base is essential to national economic growth and continued improvement in the standard of living of Australians.  The Government is committed to encouraging private enterprise to take the primary role in development of resources and to working in co-operation, not confrontation, with the States.  It has put in place policies which have a proven and internationally enviable record for:  - securing the major part of domestic energy needs.  - stimulating exploration and development in existing resource industries.  - opening up new exporting resource industries such as diamonds and liquid natural gas.  - encouraging greater domestic processing of our raw materials.  - bringing overseas investment, under proven and accepted guidelines, to "unlock" our resources while at the same time maximizing the opportunities for investment by Australians.  - ensuring that Australians receive the maximum benefits from the development of their resources.  - responding promptly to world economic pressures to maintain resources activity.  Although the resources industry has naturally been badly affected by the world recession, considerable optimism remains both in Australia and overseas about our future development prospects.  The important task now is to ensure that responsible economic and budgetary policies are continued so that our resource industries remain competitive and have the capacity to respond rapidly to any upturn in economic activity overseas.  ENERGY.  Australians must not be led to believe that the current surplus in international oil markets has removed the longer term need for a soundly-based energy policy. Australia is rich in energy resources. Proper management of those resources can ensure that we overcome the problems posed by our limited known reserve of oil and fulfil our obligations to those countries which are less well-endowed in energy resources than Australia.  This Government has pursued four fundamental goals:  - to conserve petroleum fuels to the maximum.  - to convert from oil to other energy sources (e.g. gas, electricity, coal).  - to explore vigorously for oil and gas.  - to develop the production of synthetic fuels (e.g. oil from coal and shale, ethanol from biomes, methanol and fuels from renewable sources).  OIL.  Central to the Government's energy policy is the pricing of domestic crude oil through the import parity pricing arrangements at prices comparable to what Australians would have to pay for imported supplies. That policy has encouraged increased oil exploration and development. Since it was implemented, more oil has been found than has been used, with the result that Australia's proven oil and condensate reserves are now about 500 million barrels greater than they were at June 1977. Realistic pricing of crude oil and petroleum products has also resulted in increased conservation and substitutions to other forms of energy.  This combination of discovery and conservation and the substitution of natural gas and coal-based electricity for oil in many applications has improved the outlook for self-sufficiency in liquid products. Whereas in 1979 it was estimated that, without new discoveries, Australia's degree of self-sufficiency would fall to 65% in 1985 and to 42% in 1990, it was now estimated that already discovered oil and condensate reserves will enable Australia to achieve a self-sufficiency level of about 75% in 1985 and about 47% in 1992.  There are good prospects that additional discoveries from the exploration program now under way will extend the period of relatively high self-sufficiency into the 1990s.  Under import parity pricing, Australian oil prices rise or fall in parallel with the Saudi Arabian market-price. Adjustments have customarily been made on 1 January and 1 July each year. However, to reinforce the wage pause, if the cost of imported oil falls, the Government has indicated that it will take immediate, steps to ensure that such cost reductions are passed on to the consumer.  GAS.  The Government will continue to support the development of LPG as a premium fuel particularly for automotive use. The LPG subsidy of $80 a ton has been extended to 27 March 1984 and will be sympathetically reviewed before then; this subsidy is of particular benefit to country users who do not have access to natural gas. THE APPROACH REQUIRED  The Government’s aim in its general industry policy has been:  - To provide through general economic policy, and particularly the wages pause, the means to restore competitiveness of Australian industry. It is excessive wage increases which are the main cause of the downturn in manufacturing. The Governments initiatives are the only way to ensure that manufacturing industry will emerge from the current recession soundly placed to take advantage of future opportunities.  • To provide general incentives which put Australian companies en equal footing with those overseas.  • To provide specific programs for significant industries so that they can plan their future investment with some certainty.  • To protect Australian industry from unfair trading practices by overseas competitors.  • To minimize the effect of high protection for some industries on the competitiveness and employment opportunities of other industries. NEW INITIATIVES.  In our next term in Government we intend to build on these general industry assistance measures. The Government will introduce positive and practical proposals to accelerate the development of new high technology industries; application of appropriate advanced technology in existing industries.  Australian entrepreneurs and research institutions are very good at producing innovative proposals. The problem has been translating these ideas onto the factory floor. Existing institutions and approaches have not provided a national link between the innovators and the sources of venture capital. The Government's role must be to create the framework for a national link and act as catalyst for action by the private sector.  1. THE ADVANCED TECHNOLOGY CORPORATION.  The Government will assist in the establishment of a new organization called the Advanced Technology Corporation (ADTEC), geared to developing proposals for innovative product and process development in Australia. The objectives will be to encourage the commercial development of new and more advanced products, especially those generated by small and medium size operations.  ADTEC will operate under a Board consisting of representatives of the private sector and Government. The Corporation will have three key responsibilities:  - Assessment of proposals and act as the link with venture capital and management expertise.  - A Product Development section to assist innovators and investors to locate product development facilities, and to monitor the availability and appropriateness of such facilities in Australia.  - A Market Intelligence unit to assist innovators to gain access to market research and market information services.  To ensure that the Corporation operates on commercial lines, the Board will call for tenders to manage its operations under contract for a specified period.  The Financial Co-ordination unit of the Corporation will, through the Board, license individual companies to develop particular ventures. The license will entitle the shareholders in these companies to receive a substantial tax deduction for the amount of the capital contributed. Full guidelines for  the tax deduction are being finalized. The aggregate value of licenses which the  Corporation may grant will initially be set at $100 million.  ADTEC will assist innovators to sub-contract out product development work.  Initially ADTEC will utilize existing facilities in areas such as the Institutes of Technology, CSIRO, AMDEL, and the Universities. However, if these facilities  prove inadequate the Government will take steps to expand product development  capacity.  ADTEC will also have "shop front" operations in most State capitals to maximize the access of entrepreneurs to the Corporation. The market intelligence branch will act as the initial point of contact by entrepreneurs or companies with proposals and collate and disseminate information on the availability of product development facilities, finance sources and market advice.  2. Access to our major markets will require skilled and firm negotiation by experienced negotiators if we are to secure the expansion in trade that is so vital for this country.  The initiatives the Government has taken in relation to world trade, and particularly the commitment to arrest the spread of protectionist forces have been commended by leaders of major trading countries. This Government on the basis of its past record and proven determination, has the ability to command the necessary respect so that these policies can be pursued. A traditional problem in Australia has been that Government institutions have dominated industry research. The Government is determined that the private sector develops greater research capacity. To achieve this the Government will be contracting out to industry a greater amount of the Government's research and development work.  SMALL BUSINESS  Small businesses are the backbone of the private enterprise system in Australia and are the dominant source of new employment opportunities. They also play a fundamental role in the development of smaller communities.  The Government recognizes that restoring the fundamental health of the economy is the single most important contribution to assisting small business. The Government's wages pause initiative, backed by responsible fiscal and monetary policies, will play a vital role in restoring the profitability of small businesses over the next three years.  Small businesses will also benefit from general industry assistance measures which the Government has taken in the last year.  UNDERSTANDING SMALL BUSINESS.  The diversity of small business needs special understanding.  To overcome this the Government established a Small Business Advisory Council in 1978 which acts as a valuable link between Government and small business.  The Council is to prepare a comprehensive report on small business in Australia which will draw together all available data on small business.  In addition, the Bureau of Industry Economics has devoted a, substantial effort to upgrading research and information about small business in Australia.  With the help of these two bodies and others including the Council of Small  Business Organizations of Australia, the Government has identified a number of issues of particular concern to small business and has taken positive steps to address them.  TAXATION.  Small firms rely to a significant extent on internally generated funds for growth and development.  Since assuming office the Government has:  - increased from 50% to 80% the proportion of after tax trading profit which a private company may retain free of undistributed profits (Division 7) tax.  - introduced a rebate on eligible dividend income up to $1000.  - abolished estate and gift duty.  The Government also introduced new superannuating provisions to encourage self-employed businessmen to make greater provision for their retirement.  The Government has now decided to introduce from 1983/84 a preferential income tax rate of 41% for small businesses with taxable incomes up to $100000 with special shading-in arrangements on incomes of up to $150000.  FINANCE.  Access to long term and equity finance has been a significant problem for many small businesses, especially those which are innovative and rapidly growing.  Through the Reserve Bank the Government has made known to the banking sector its desire that adequate finance be available for small business enterprises in Australia. The Government has supported recent decisions by Westpac and Citicorp to set up special facilities for small business.  In 1978 the Government extended the charter of the Commonwealth Development Bank and the Bank's non-rural lending is now directed almost entirely to small business undertakings. In the four years to June 1982 the Bank lent over $100 million to small businesses. In December the Government took steps to improve access to finance for small business through the Bank.  The Government wishes to further extend the capacity of the Commonwealth Development Bank to assist small businesses. It will therefore provide $25 million by way of a loan for a special division within the Commonwealth Development Bank to cater specifically for the financial needs of small business.  MANAGEMENT ASSISTANCE AND AWARENESS.  To help upgrade the level of management expertise the Government has increased its support for training and management education services available to small business. The Government will expand its efforts in this field as the opportunity arises.  We will also continue our support for the national Small Business Awards Program which we introduced in 1979. The program, which is run in association with the Confederation of Australian Industry and the Australian Chamber of Commerce, is designed to enhance public awareness of the importance of small business to the Australian community.  PROTECTION OF THE SMALL BUSINESSMAN.  Unfair competition from big businesses can be a problem for the small businessman.  The Government has legislated to protect the interests of franchisees in retail petroleum marketing and is considering whether general legislation should be introduced for the protection of franchisees.  TOURISM  Tourism is one of Australia's growth industries and will remain so throughout the 1980s.  Industry studies have forecast that tourist expenditure could increase by $1 billion by 1983, and lead to the creation of 30 000 new jobs.  GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO TOURIST INDUSTRY.  The Government will join with the industry in a national effort to develop a growth strategy for the tourist industry in the 1980s. PRIMARY INDUSTRY  This Government recognizes the vital importance of our primary industry to the national economy. Agricultural products account for nearly half of our total export earnings. The Government continues to be committed to ensuring a strong and efficient rural sector. We have vigorously sought to improve and open new international markets for our products. We will continue to do so most forcefully at every opportunity. The Government commissioned a major report by the Balderstone Committee on Agriculture in Australia and it will draw on the recommendations in that report to formulate future policies for rural industries.  MEASURES TO DEAL WITH THE EFFECTS OF THE DROUGHT.  This Government has always stood ready to help rural industries, where and when such assistance is necessary. No better example of this can be found than in the current drought assistance measures. The Commonwealth has allocated $356 million this financial year to two specific Commonwealth measures - the Fodder and Interest Payments Subsidies.  These are in addition to drought aid available under the Natural Disaster Relief Arrangements. Overall, the drought aid measures are the most comprehensive ever introduced in Australia. They recognize the farmer's immediate needs, and his longer term requirements.  The continuing drought poses one of the most serious threats that our primary industries have ever seen. Clearly, farmers' problems will not end simply when the drought breaks.  We will therefore extend the Commonwealth Interest Payments Subsidy for one year beyond the lifting of drought declarations. This will cost an estimated $7 million in 1983/84, and will greatly assist farmers with their debt repayments in the post drought period.  We have already asked the Industries Assistance Commission to report by the end of April on how the Rural Adjustment Scheme might best be used to help farmers restructure their properties and debts in light of the drought. We will act urgently on that report to ensure adequate funding is available in the Rural Adjustment Scheme for this purpose, and ensure there are financial arrangements for assisting with planting crops including carry-on loans.  Under the Natural Disaster Relief Arrangements, we will provide an additional $12 million in 1983/84 to ensure that adequate funding is available to primary producers for restocking purposes.  We will lift Commonwealth contributions to Rural Research in 1983/84 from $22.5 million to $30 million. Research will be undertaken to help farmers reduce costs in times of drought, in areas such as drought tolerant pastures, efficient water use in irrigation and effective fertilizer practice.  Soil conservation is another area of particular concern in the drought context, and was also the subject of recommendations by the Balderstone Committee. The Government has always maintained a commitment to soil conservation through specific tax concessions to farmers and grants to the States.  We will now implement a National Soil Conservation Program, to which the Commonwealth will provide $5 million in 1983/84, rising to $15 million annually by 1987/88.  In addition to these measures, inland Australia stands to benefit greatly from the Government's recently announced National Water Resources Program, under which $640 million will be spent over the next five years. In co-operation with the State and Territory governments the Commonwealth Government has developed a wide range of programs of environmental protection and nature conservation.  The Government has recently passed the Wildlife Protection (Regulation of Exports and Imports) Act which will ensure that Australia's unique wildlife, both plants and animals, are protected from illegal exports, and from the risk of importing exotic species which might harm Australian native species. It will link Darwin to the national railway network, boost the development of the Northern Territory, and make a significant contribution to Australia's defense capability. The Government will provide $105 million over three years to undertake economically justified projects on rail links to major export ports.  SHIPPING.  The Government has introduced measures to revitalize Australia's shipping industry in line with the recommendations of the Crawford Committee of Inquiry. Revised taxation arrangements for Australian ship owners whose ships meet appropriate manning levels place Australian shipping on the same fiscal basis as international shipping. This initiative will provide an opportunity to Australia's shipping industry to compete on equitable terms with the ships of other nations.  The Government has expressly rejected cargo reservation in overseas trades as a means of forcing entry of Australian ships into the overseas trades.  We will continue the process of deregulation of import controls on ships in the interests of increased competition and improving the efficiency of coastal shipping.  Given the important role the Australian Shippers' Council plays in the negotiation of Australia's overseas freight rates, government assistance to the Council will be increased.  PORTS.  The Government will proceed to connect the standard-gauge railway to the ports of Melbourne, Geelong and Fisherman's Island (Qld), in consultation with the States.  The Government will also proceed to connect the standard gauge railway from Tocumwal on the NSW/Vic border to Mangalore which will ensure that there will be a standard gauge connection between the Riverina and NSW generally to the Port of Geelong.  The Government will maintain the Tasmanian Freight Equalization Scheme under the existing Nimmo concept. The Government will also introduce a system which allows industry to request reviews of the levels of assistance. Such reviews will be requested through the Minister for Transport and Construction and undertaken by the Bureau of Transport Economics.  The Government will maintain the sea passenger and freight services link with Tasmania. We will work with the Tasmanian Government to determine the most appropriate and efficient means of providing the service.  We will strengthen civil co-ordination arrangements to ensure effective surveillance of Australia's coast, particularly our northern coastline, the Great Barrier Reef and Bass Strait.  Responsibility for our coastal surveillance system will clearly rest with the Department of Transport and Construction.  We will, in co-operation with the States, provide assistance to voluntary Coastguard services, who play a vital role in our National Search and Rescue efforts.  NAVIGATION AIDS.  The Government has decided to provide adequate navigation aids in the Hydrographers Passage in the waters of the Great Barrier Reef to shorten the shipping route for the export of coal, minerals and other goods from Queensland to northbound ports. This decision will help to make our export industries from Central Queensland more competitive. The family is the most fundamental and important social and cohesive force in society. The Government's concern to secure the position of families has been reflected in the range of changes to education, housing, taxation and social security and welfare programs introduced in the 1982/83 Budget. The Government has also responded to the special needs of sole parents and disabled people of all ages. Our past achievements represent a base from which we will continue to build. HOUSING  The housing industry is now emerging from a difficult period during which interest rates around the world rose to record levels.  The Government recognizes that home ownership is a unique aspect of Australian family life. Around 70 per cent of Australians own their own home compared with 50 per cent in the UK and 62 per cent in Canada.  With this in mind, the Government has reacted quickly and effectively to ease the impact of high interest rates on home owners and stimulate activity in the industry.  A comprehensive housing package was presented in March 1982 and this was enhanced in the 1982/83 Budget. Further measures have followed since the Budget.  These initiatives have fallen in four main areas:  1. HOME LOAN INTEREST REBATE.  All people paying off their own home can now claim a tax rebate of 30c in the dollar on interest over 10% on the first $60000 of a loan for buildings or extensions of principal residence. First home buyers can claim rebates up to a maximum of $700 in interest where this confers a larger rebate.  2. HOME DEPOSITS ASSISTANCE.  The Government decided to replace the Home Savings Grant Scheme with a Home Deposit Assistance Scheme in March 1982.  Home Deposit Assistance Grants are payable, subject to a family income test, to assist with the purchase or construction of a first home. A maximum basic grant of $2500 is payable in respect of savings held for two years ending on the contract date. In addition to the basic grant, the Scheme provides for a family bonus of $500 for families with one dependent child and $1000 for families with two or more dependent children.  The new scheme provides significant improvements over the old home savings grants scheme including:  - an increase in the basic maximum grant from $200 to $2500.  - relaxation of savings conditions.  - abolition of the house value limit.  - abolition of the nine month waiting period.  3. AGREEMENTS WITH THE MAJOR BANKS.  Australia's major banks made commitments to the Government in March  1982 that they would increase their home lending by $400 million in the year ending March 1983. That commitment has since been extended to March 1984 and the banks have indicated to the Government that they would attempt to increase home lending further if conditions in the financial markets permitted. The major banks have also given commitments to improve the flexibility in repayment periods for certain new home loans and develop special arrangements designed to assist first home buyers including facilities such as low start mortgages.  4. WELFARE HOUSING.  The Government allocated $333 million for welfare housing programs in the States in the 1982/83 Budget. HEALTH  Government policies aim to:  - ensure all Australians have access to good quality health care.  - maintain the right of choice while ensuring those individuals who can afford it contribute to their own health care.  - ensure health insurance is available to all at a reasonable cost.  - provide special assistance for those in need including pensioners, the chronically ill and the disadvantaged.  - encourage the States to accept full responsibility for their own health care systems.  - promote care within the community rather than in hospitals.  - promote preventive health measures.  The changes to health financing and the health insurance introduced by the Government have contributed to a more efficient and responsive health care system. Individuals have been encouraged to take responsibility for their own health care needs directly or through health insurance. Providers of health services have been given more incentives for excellence and efficiency. To encourage a broadly based system of health insurance, the Government introduced a tax rebate at standard rate for the cost of basic hospital and medical insurance with registered health funds. In 1982/83 tax rebates provided are estimated to exceed $500 million.  The Government's new arrangements have concentrated assistance on those moss in need:  - 20% of Australians have free health care.  - eligible pensioners and the socially disadvantaged have free access to public hospitals.  - the Government also pays medical benefits for eligible pensioners and their dependants; migrants and refugees within their first six months in Australia; unemployed and special beneficiaries who meet the Pensioner Health Benefit Income test; and other people who meet a specified income test.  - Commonwealth has also taken over full responsibility for payment of nursing home benefits for all qualified people at a cost of over $534 million in 1982/83.  In the 1982/83 Budget the Government:  - increased the limits on non-pension income from November 1982 for Pensioner Health Benefits Cardholders to $54 a week single and $90 a week married.  - introduced new patient contribution arrangements under the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme to assist an additional 1.3.million Australians with a new reduced rate. The Government recognizes the important part the private hospitals have in health care.
